summary:
In Indonesia's fire seasons, the two groups closest to a fire each see half the picture. Fire officers have NASA hotspots from MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m), but the two records cannot be compared directly: in our archive, adding VIIRS multiplies post-2012 counts about five times with no real increase in fire. Residents see smoke and flames first, but those we interviewed said information reaches them only after a fire has started, and many do not know where to report.

AGNIBHŪMI is a web application that joins these halves. It harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS into one burning-activity calendar for Indonesia (2000–2026), flags unusual months and critical periods for any chosen area, and ranks areas for officers to check first. Residents see nearby hotspots, wind and air quality, and can report a fire with a location and photo. Each report is automatically matched with satellite detections within 5 km and 24 hours, then reviewed by an officer, so ground observations and satellite data check each other. A hotspot is never presented as a confirmed fire.
details:
The problem, and how AGNIBHŪMI answers it

Three gaps keep fire information from being useful early. Each one maps to a part of the app.

  1. Officers have satellite data they cannot read as one record. MODIS and VIIRS differ in pixel size, overpass time and confidence format. An officer cannot tell whether today is normal for an area, or which of thousands of points to check first. Answer: the harmonized calendar gives one comparable history, flags unusual months and critical periods, and the priority list orders areas with the reasons shown.
  2. Residents see fire first but have no channel. Residents we interviewed said they learn about a fire only after it has started, and many do not know where to report. Answer: the Community view shows an area status, nearest hotspots, wind direction and air quality for the resident's own location, and a report form that takes a location, a category and one photo, with an emergency-call button at the top.
  3. Satellites and people never meet. Satellites pass only a few times a day and cannot see through thick cloud or smoke, so some fires go undetected for hours. Residents can fill that gap, but an unverified report is hard for an officer to trust. Answer: every citizen report is matched automatically with satellite detections within 5 km and 24 hours and shown to an officer, who decides its status. The satellite gives the report an independent check; the report gives the satellite eyes on the ground. Once verified, the report raises the area status for nearby residents.

Citizen reporting is therefore not an add-on. It is the link that turns a satellite record into something both officers and residents can act on.

What it does

AGNIBHŪMI answers the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" with five things:

  1. Harmonized detections. It pulls near-real-time data from four FIRMS feeds (MODIS, VIIRS S-NPP, VIIRS NOAA-20, VIIRS NOAA-21), cleans them, and pairs each MODIS detection with the nearest VIIRS detection within 10 km and 12 hours. A matched pair counts as one event.
  2. Burning activity calendar. A month-by-year heatmap built from the FIRMS archive (2000–2026) plus live data for the current month. It offers two series: "Comparable" (MODIS only, one sensor family across the whole record) and "Detailed" (MODIS + VIIRS, from 2012).
  3. Unusual conditions and critical periods. A month is flagged unusual when it exceeds the mean plus two standard deviations of the same month in other years. Critical periods are months averaging at least 1.5 times a normal month. Nationally this gives August–October, which holds 69% of yearly events in our archive.
  4. Area of interest. All calendar numbers can be recomputed for a province, district, sub-district, or a polygon the user draws on the map. Results can be downloaded as CSV.
  5. Two audiences on one backend. The Operator view adds a priority list with its formula shown, citizen-report review, and an incident workflow (human verification, manual priority, team assignment, progress, with every change recorded with its reason on a timeline that cannot be edited). The Community view shows an area status, nearest hotspots, wind, air quality, educational content, and a report form with an emergency-call button.

How it works

  • A Python service (FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, Shapely) fetches FIRMS data, removes invalid coordinates, negative FRP and duplicate rows, and keeps nominal and high confidence detections (MODIS ≥ 30%, VIIRS "n" or "h").
  • The 12-hour matching window was chosen after measuring our data: pairs less than 1 km apart were often 2–15 hours apart, because the two sensors pass over at different times.
  • The archive is aggregated to daily counts per 0.25° grid cell (1,069,505 rows) in SQLite.
  • "Unusual today" compares live counts with each cell's own history for the same season, using the same sensor population on both sides. When that is not possible the page says "cannot be compared yet" instead of substituting other satellites.
  • Citizen reports are automatically linked to satellite detections within 5 km and 24 hours. The link never changes a report's status; an officer decides.
  • A Next.js front end (React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Leaflet) only displays what the backend computed. The interface is available in Indonesian and English.
  • Officer accounts and the incident workflow run on Supabase (Auth and Postgres). Each officer signs in with an individual account and a role; row-level security and validated database functions enforce who can change what, and version checks stop two officers from overwriting each other.
  • The repository includes 130 Python tests, 22 database access-rule tests, and an end-to-end test that follows a citizen report through to an incident.

Benefits

  • Years can be compared without mistaking a new sensor for more fire.
  • Officers get a reasoned order of areas to check, with the factors shown (FRP, consecutive active days, seen by both sensors).
  • Residents get earlier, plain-language information about their own surroundings. This was the main request in our interviews.
  • Privacy is built in: other residents only see officer-verified reports, with coordinates rounded to about 1 km and no photo; photo metadata is stripped; officer pages require an individual officer account with a role.

What we hope to achieve

We want fire responders such as Manggala Agni and local disaster agencies to spend less time interpreting two sensor records and more time deciding where to verify. We want residents to learn about nearby fire activity before it reaches them. Next steps are validating the priority weights with responders, adding NOAA-20 archive data now that Suomi NPP has stopped delivering new data, and sending early warnings as push notifications.

How we reduce false readings

A hotspot is a thermal anomaly, so the app layers four checks instead of treating any single detection as fire: (1) low-confidence detections are removed (MODIS below 30%, VIIRS "low"); (2) a detection seen by both MODIS and VIIRS is marked as matched; (3) repeated detections on consecutive days raise an area's priority; (4) citizen reports near a detection, reviewed by an officer, provide the only ground evidence. None of these confirms a fire on its own. Persistent industrial heat sources can also pass the first three, which is why human verification remains the final step.

Honest limits

  • A hotspot is a thermal anomaly, not a confirmed fire, and a day without detections is not a day without fire (cloud and smoke hide fires).
  • The priority score is a fixed formula, not AI, and its weights have not been validated with fire agencies. We do not estimate fire risk.
  • Thresholds (2 standard deviations, 1.5 times) are our own choices and are stated on the page.
  • The smallest unit is a 0.25° cell (about 27 km), so small areas can include fire from just outside them.
  • Air quality uses US AQI, not Indonesia's ISPU scale.

Tools, languages and software

Python 3.12, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, Shapely, Pillow, pytest, SQLite; Supabase (Auth, Postgres with row-level security); TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, React-Leaflet and Zod; Playwright for end-to-end tests; Docker; Vercel and Render for hosting; Figma for interface design; Miro for research and planning; Git and GitHub.

How it is creative

Most fire tools either show satellite points or manage field operations. AGNIBHŪMI connects the two with a third source: residents. A citizen report is matched with satellite detections automatically, so each source checks the other. We also keep two calendar series side by side instead of merging the sensors into one number, which lets users compare years honestly and still see VIIRS detail.

What we considered

We chose not to predict or confirm fires, because a hotspot is only a thermal anomaly. We measured our own data before fixing the 12-hour matching window. We protected reporters by showing other residents only officer-verified reports with rounded coordinates and no photo. We kept every threshold and formula visible on the page so officers can question them.
